La resta y la división <strong>no</stron: Subtraction and division are not commutative: $7-3 \ne 3-7$ and $10:2 \ne 2:10$. It is the most repeated error of the whole of secondary school.
La distributiva es la que más rendimient: The distributive law is the one that pays off most, and the one most often applied wrongly. It says that multiplying by a sum is the same as multiplying by each addend and adding afterwards: $5\cdot(10 + 2) = 5\cdot 10 + 5\cdot 2 = 60$. Read it from right to left too, which is how it is used to take out a common factor: $5\cdot 10 + 5\cdot 2 = 5\cdot(10 + 2)$.

Que sumar se pueda hacer en cualquier or: That adding can be done in any order is what allows an enormous calculation to be shared among many processors: each one adds its piece and then they are put together. Now the small print, which surprises many an engineer: with decimals stored in a computer the associative law stops holding exactly. Adding a million data items in a different order can give different results in the last digits, and in climate or structural simulations that forces the order to be fixed so that results are reproducible.

Esta prioridad no es un capricho escolar: This priority is not a schoolroom whim: it is exactly the one applied by a spreadsheet, a calculator and any programming language when reading a formula. That is why a badly written cell gives a plausible but wrong result, with no warning. And the arguments that go round social media with expressions like $8 \div 2(2+2)$ are not a mathematics problem but an ambiguous-notation one: with one more bracket, the discussion disappears.

El orden de las operaciones no lo dictó: The order of operations was not dictated by any mathematician: it settled in with the printing press between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, for typographical convenience. Since polynomials were written constantly, it was practical for $3x^2$ to mean “three times x squared” without needing brackets. In other words, the hierarchy taught today as if it were a law of nature is really a printers' convention that stuck.
